title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
description:
# Largest Rectangle in Histogram

You are given an integer array `heights`, where `heights[i]` is the height of the `i`th bar in a histogram. Every bar has width `1`.

A rectangle in the histogram must be formed by one or more consecutive bars. Its height is limited by the shortest bar it spans, and its width is the number of bars it spans.

Return the area of the largest rectangle that can be formed in the histogram.

## Example 1:

**Input:** heights = [2,1,5,6,2,3]
**Output:** 10
**Explanation:** The best rectangle spans the bars with heights 5 and 6. Its height is 5 and its width is 2, so its area is 10.

## Example 2:

**Input:** heights = [2,4]
**Output:** 4
**Explanation:** The best area is either the bar of height 4 alone, or both bars with limiting height 2.

## Constraints:

*   `1 <= heights.length <= 10^5`
*   `0 <= heights[i] <= 10^4`

tests.description: Canonical histogram with interior maximum rectangle
Two bars where either one tall bar or both bars can be optimal
Middle valley limits a rectangle spanning all bars
Zero-height bar splits the histogram into independent regions
All bars have the same height
Strictly increasing heights need a final stack flush
Strictly decreasing heights pop on every step
Wide plateau beats the taller middle bar
Upper height boundary with area larger than a single bar

solutions.name: Monotonic Increasing Stack
solutions.description:
## Approach

Maintain a stack of bar indices whose heights are in increasing order. When the current bar is shorter than the bar at the stack top, pop the taller bar and compute the largest rectangle where that popped bar is the limiting height. Use a virtual height `0` after the last bar to flush the stack.

## Key Insight

A bar's maximum rectangle is known exactly when we find the first shorter bar to its right. After popping it, the new stack top is the first shorter bar to its left, so the width is determined immediately.

## Complexity Analysis

Each index is pushed and popped at most once.

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Precomputed Smaller Boundaries
solutions.description:
## Approach

For every bar, precompute the nearest strictly smaller bar on the left and on the right. If bar `i` is the limiting height, it can span from `left[i] + 1` through `right[i] - 1`. Compute that area for every bar and take the maximum.

## Key Insight

This is the same boundary invariant as the monotonic stack solution, but stored explicitly. It is useful for teaching because each bar's width can be inspected directly.

## Complexity Analysis

Two monotonic stack passes find all boundaries, followed by one area pass.

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Divide and Conquer with Segment Tree
solutions.description:
## Approach

Build a segment tree that returns the index of the minimum-height bar in any range. For a range `[left, right]`, the minimum bar gives the best rectangle spanning the whole range. Then split around that minimum bar and process the left and right subranges.

## Key Insight

Every optimal rectangle either spans the minimum bar of the current range, lies completely to its left, or lies completely to its right. The segment tree keeps the minimum-index query fast, and an explicit range stack avoids recursion depth issues on sorted inputs.

## Complexity Analysis

The segment tree uses linear space and answers range-minimum queries in logarithmic time.

- Time Complexity: O(n log n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Quadratic Minimum Scan Baseline
solutions.description:
## Approach

Enumerate every possible left boundary. As the right boundary expands, keep the minimum height inside the current window. That minimum height times the window width is the best rectangle for this exact span.

## Key Insight

This baseline mirrors the definition of the problem: each candidate rectangle is a consecutive span limited by its shortest bar. The faster stack solutions are ways to avoid repeating the same minimum-height work for many spans.

## Complexity Analysis

There are O(n^2) spans, so this is only a teaching baseline, not the intended large-input solution.

- Time Complexity: O(n^2)
- Space Complexity: O(1)
